title: What Persuasion Really Is
author: Andrea Chiarelli
source: The Art of Asking Questions (Andrea Chiarelli)
summary: Andrea Chiarelli summarizes a conversation with Josh, author of 'How to Get What You Want,' exploring what persuasion actually is and why most people mistake winning arguments for persuading others. Josh opens with Daryl Davis -- a Black blues musician who persuaded over 200 KKK members to leave the organization by sitting with them and asking: 'How can you hate me if you don't even know me?' This cuts against the instinct to out-argue opponents. The Latin root of 'convince' means to vanquish or conquer; Josh reframes persuasion as shared action aimed at getting something done together. The article explains why human wiring works against persuasion -- we feel first, reason second, lean negative, and default to our own values rather than our counterpart's. Three types of listening are distinguished: passive (making the other feel heard), active (going deeper into what they said), and proactive (asking how they want to move forward). Persuasion differs from manipulation primarily in intent, and its practical test is the 'granny test': if your grandmother cannot understand what you are saying, the communication failure is yours.
points: * Daryl Davis persuaded 200+ KKK members to leave the organization not through argument but through relationship -- sitting down, asking genuine questions, and making them feel known. * The Latin root of 'convince' means to vanquish; treating a conversation as conquest means the best you can hope for is that the other person walks away feeling like they lost. * Josh frames persuasion as shared action -- something we choose to do with others, aimed at getting something done together, not something we do to them. * Human wiring works against persuasion: we feel first and reason second, we tend toward negativity, and we instinctively reach for our own values rather than our counterpart's. * The three listening types -- passive (making the other feel heard), active (going deeper), and proactive (asking how they want to move forward) -- form a ladder of increasing persuasive power.
quotes: In any encounter, do you want to be right, or do you want to make a difference?
The two are not the same thing, and most of the time they pull in opposite directions.
The Latin root of 'convince' actually means to vanquish or conquer, and if you treat a conversation as conquest, the best you can hope for is that the other person walks away feeling like they lost.
Josh prefers to think of persuasion as shared action, something we choose to do with others, aimed at getting something done together.

Listening is not the same as agreeing, and it is not the same as staying silent. The goal is to make your counterpart feel understood: this is rare enough that, when you achieve it, trust tends to follow.
Persuasion and manipulation differ primarily in your intentions -- and people can sense them.
If your grandmother cannot understand what you are saying, you have not communicated it well enough. And that is your problem, not hers.
